This is everything I want to see in indie game of this kind : many build possibilities, interesting combos, a lot of replayability, a leaderboard system that makes the player want to get better, with just enough competitive system that won't frustrate you if you're not really into it. Moreover, and it's a very important point : an invested dev team that actively listens to their community feedbacks, always make their best to keep the game balanced and satisfy the players in what we expect in this kind of game. A lot more is coming and I'm really looking forward the new heroes and mechanics we will get in the future !

This game saved my life. I am 39. My ex-wife and I have a daughter together, and adopted our son together. They are now both 4 years old. When we were going through our separation, I found myself lost and miserable. I was self destructive. I got so mad one day from everything spiraling out of my control that I punched some concrete in a moment of overwhelming emotion. That caused me to break my 5th metacarpal in my right hand... my working hand... my games hand.. the hand that I held and carried my children to bed with.. The hand I desperately needed to make sure I could continue to provide. After learning of the severity of my self-inflicted damage, I was borderline suicidal. Keep in mind that just a few months before this, I was the happiest man with no history of depression or anxiety. I have never had fits of rage, or been one to break down and cry, but I was in a low spot that just really buried me from being able to see the light on the other side. Having nothing better to do, I searched for a game I could play, ONE HANDED while I recovered. I somehow stumbled upon this game and read some of the reviews. I decided that it had to be worth a shot... I must admit, I didn't beat the game, or play nearly as long as some of you. In fact, I may have only played this game a day or two.. With that being said, after doing so, I had a new found joy and hope for life. I was able to put behind me the pain and suffering that had been cast over me. I was able to experience other peoples joy and happiness. I was able to see the fruits of my "labor". I relaxed for 5 ♥♥♥♥ing minutes to this music long enough to realize that I was going to be okay. After coming to that realization, I turned the game off, and I went back to work. It hurt my hand like hell but I was motivated. I stopped feeling so damn sorry for myself, and I became the father I needed to be in that moment, not the weak boy I was behaving as. Today, I am close friend with my kids mother. We don't fight, or argue, or say hurtful things to each other. We are parents, and friends. I now have 3 kids. My third child is, wait for it, ALSO 4 YEARS OLD. The woman I am with was going through a very similar situation at the time of my own separation, and we just stumbled in to each others life unexpectedly. We have been in a relationship for a year now, and are very happy together. Moral of the story, you never know what life holds in store for you, and if I would have given up when all the odds were stacked against me, I wouldn't be where I am today. This silly little game helped me realize that. Thank you.

UPDATE: The original version of this review suggests that only winning builds are saved for general play. Though a representative for 1TK confirmed to Summit that user-created boards can face one another regardless of winning outside of the Duel mode, the version of the game as we covered it in our Early Access review could be seen as saying otherwise. Please see the dev comment on this review for a clarification of the board save state. ORIGINAL REVIEW: Turnbound takes the challenge of building an autobattler in a bit of a different direction, though how successful it is in doing so is open to debate. Turnbound is a board game-esque auto-battler. You play as one of three characters—Sun Wukong, Alice from Alice in Wonderland, and Robin Hood—each with their own unique abilities and desired combos. Players then buy tiles to place on their boards, creating a web of potential combos and strategies, all with the singular goal of annihilating their opponent. Players win when they reach ten victories against other players’ saved state boards, and lose when they run out of lives. That each character has their own abilities gives each of the three characters their own strategy and feel. Playing Alice, for example, my primary goal is to chain enough potions that I win before my opponent has even really had a turn, with their first action triggering my special ability multiple times over. Playing Robin Hood, on the other hand, I don’t care about potions, instead finding ways to destroy tiles and donating the resulting coins to power up my own massive abilities. https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3656262777 However, while each character has their own specific feel and strategy, they do have access to a common pool of tiles. As Robin Hood, it’s possible for me to draw tiles intended for Sun Wukong, and vice versa, creating the potential for combinations beyond the expected. There are, as always, pros and cons to this. On the one hand, having a broad pool of shared items means items that work well in one build can potentially be adapted to another. On the other hand, the large number of items means one particular item, that could be vital for a particular build, can be hard to find. Or, more frustratingly, that any items that fit a particular character and their abilities don’t show up for multiple turns, leading to a near-guaranteed loss. It’s in the tiles and the mechanics within them that some of the flaws with the game design itself appear, making it clear how unintentionally frustrating this game can be. https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3656263411 Take, for instance, the process of acquiring tiles. The game alternates between battles and shops, with each shop being an opportunity to buy new tiles and new board spaces, and rearrange or upgrade the items already on the board. Players receive a limited number of coins with which to do these things—in the above example, I have twelve coins—with any leftover coins carrying over to the next round. Upgrading items requires having multiple of the same item, plus an extra coin to pay for the process of upgrading, and each board square costs a coin to unlock. One immediate flaw is that there are not enough coins to upgrade boards in what feels like meaningful ways, especially with characters and builds that incentivise having a large number of objects. In the above example, for instance, my twelve coins vanish before my board meaningfully changes, with seven coins purchasing a hero upgrade, another coin applying the upgrade, and the remaining four coins either purchasing board space or a single object, leaving me with more or less the same board state as I move into the next battle. While some objects do offer the ability to generate coins within a battle, these objects are both rare and generate a negligible amount of coins. The ultimate consequence of this lack of resources is that, while it encourages players to think strategically about their purchases, it also disincentivises experimentation and switching strategies over the course of a run. When buying and placing one object potentially runs through the entirety of the resources I have available for that turn, there is little incentive for me to change my build, especially when it’s unclear whether my build will actually benefit from having done so. If the first shop I see doesn’t have something immediately helpful, rerolling is also expensive enough to disincentivise exploring to see if there’s something better. Turnbound’s economy, then, disincentivises what I would consider to be one of the fundamental joys of deckbuilders and auto-battlers specifically. There is no space to experiment and to see if a new, unknown card can make numbers go brrrr. https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3656263973 While the economy design alone disincentivises experimentation, there is a more fundamental element of Turnbound’s game design that removes more of the joy of deckbuilding. Turnbound is nominally a multiplayer game. While there is no way for players to play against one another live, battles are played against another player’s saved board. However, unlike other saved state auto-battlers, Turnbound only saves the boards of the players who successfully win ten battles, with battles then being played against these boards at their various stages of victory. Unsuccessful boards—whether they win nine battles or zero—are not saved. In the long-run, this also leads to the game becoming inaccessible to new players. When the only boards available to play against are those who have won, there is an endless power creep, with builds needing to be ever more efficient to survive even at the lowest levels. Setting aside the lack of room for exploration, Turnbound’s design will, if left unchecked, eventually create a game that’s unplayable to any but the absolute luckiest. It is deeply deterministic in a way that isn’t true of most deckbuilders or even auto-battlers. Recovering from a couple of bad rounds is nearly impossible, and the strategies for doing so are limited at best. That said, Turnbound still brings something unique to the auto-battler table. Its approach of a board covered with tiles is an interesting one, and placing tiles strategically is a fun challenge all on its own. There is a satisfaction in watching a chain reaction win me the battle before it’s even begun, knowing that I have indeed placed every element of that chain correctly. It is also worth considering that Turnbound is still in Early Access. While the game, as it currently stands, has flaws, none of these flaws are necessarily fundamental. There is enough potential within Turnbound that it is a game worth watching, even though its current state leaves a bit to be desired. While any individual run may be fun, anyone seeking something that allows the freedom that traditionally accompanies auto-battlers may want to wait and see how the game develops. There are elements of Turnbound that are creative, unique, and interesting. There is potential here for an interesting auto-battler with fresh takes on strategic thinking within the genre. Instead, Turnbound is hobbled by designs that punish precisely the sort of creative thinking that draws players to deckbuilders in the first place. This is a game I want to enjoy, but it’s difficult when every round looks exactly the same as the one that came before, and I’m left staring at things I want to build, but can never afford to try. As someone with over 100 hours in Backpack Battles, I can't recommend this game in its current state. There are several specific balancing problems: 1: Economy: As mentioned by other reviews, there are often many turns where you are left without much to do because the cost of items is way too high in general. For instance, if I wanted to buy a 3 or 4 slot item, which average around 6-8 cost or so, you might as well add on an additional 3-4 coin cost to afford the board space needed to accommodate that item. When you are receiving 12-13 coins a round, this often means you are purchasing a single item to change your board state on quite a few rounds. This sucks. This problem is compounded by the dupe system by which items are upgraded by fusing them with the same item, which then grants you a bonus random item for your trouble. So some turns you will be offered a dupe in your opening shop refresh, and the obvious choice is to just buy that dupe. There is no thought on the part of the player, it is obviously the best choice to dupe to scale power and get a free item. 2: Adjacency: The vast majority of items that are not weapons/armor require items to be adjacent to themselves to be effective. This is, frankly, boring to see repeated on every item ad nauseum, and frustrating to try and fit everything around to work properly. Also: unlike Backpack Battles where you can freely arrange the position and orientation of your bags, tile unlocks are permanent and cannot be shuffled around. This feeds into the economy issue where even if you have space for a new item, if it isn't the correctly shaped space you will still be required to purchase more space to accommodate that new item. 3: Scaling: By far my biggest issue with the game. It feels like a lot of strategy and build ideas either current or future will be irrelevant because it is too easy to scale power on weapons to the point that any hit on an opposing tile will oneshot that tile (This can start happening as early as turn 4!!!). This ends up turning midgame-endgame boards into a game of "how many taunts can I assemble that each soak an attack" while you one-shot anything you hit. On-hit status effects like Poison, Sleep, and Remove Taunt rarely matter when you one-shot anything you touch. Alice was my favorite hero to play out of the 3 options, and it's infuriating how many items she has that are rendered useless by this balance. So many consumables and armors and whatnot that trigger when damaged or when taken to 50% health or less, that don't matter because of how consistently items are one-shot. Generally speaking, I also found that items of high rarity are often underwhelming. A 2 or 3 duped item of the lowest rarity is almost always going to do more damage (weapon) or soak more damage(armor) than an un-duped copy of a higher rarity item. The abilities on higher rarity equipment often do not make up the difference. And to tie it back into Problem 2: Turns out it's even more boring when all of those "adjacency matters" tiles all just scale HP and power in different ways. In conclusion: I genuinely wanted to like this game, hungry for new autobattlers as I am, but I just can't recommend this game right now. It isn't doing anything unique compared to other autobattlers and it isn't doing anything better than them either.

As a hardcore veteran of Hearthstone, Slay the Spire, Balatro, and For the King, this game, even in its current developing stage, has already joined the ranks among my favorite strategy games. It has, in my opinion, achieved infinite depth and huge strategic variety while sticking to simple and intuitive game mechanics. These are the qualities of a great strategy game. I will say, though, that, as it is with any roguelikes, it is possible to fall into the trap of a perceived rigidity, by defaulting to a familiar strategy. For example, I kept fusing tiles whenever I could (it is very tempting to do so). But not all fusions are meaningfully useful, and some tiles are better off being used as separate low tier tiles, depending on context. Once I realized that, I was able to pull off some crazy builds, and have also faced opponents with crazy builds. I can promise that this game allows for the craziest builds and synergies, if you approach it with an open mind. Anyways, 10/10 for me.

Turnbound is a game that respects your intelligence. It doesn’t hold your hand, and it doesn’t let you win by luck. It is a minimalist tactical RPG that strips away the fluff and focuses entirely on the "purity" of the turn-based encounter. If you are a fan of games where a single square of movement determines life or death, this is exactly what you’ve been looking for. [b]The Gameplay Experience[/b] The game feels like a dark, high-stakes board game. You aren't just clicking buttons; you are solving a combat puzzle. Every enemy has a clear behavior, and learning those patterns is incredibly rewarding. The progression system is tight, allowing you to specialize your character without overwhelming you with useless stats. [b]The Plus Side[/b] [b]Meaningful Strategy:[/b] There is almost zero RNG (randomness) here. If you lose, it’s because you made a mistake, not because the game cheated you. That makes the victories feel earned. [b]Atmospheric Art Style:[/b] The dark, minimalist aesthetic is fantastic. It creates a "grim-dark" mood that keeps you focused on the tension of the dungeon. [b]No Time Wasted:[/b] The game respects your time. There are no 20-minute unskippable cutscenes—you jump straight into the tactical action. [b]Tactile Feedback:[/b] For an indie game, the "feel" of the combat is surprisingly weighty and satisfying. [b]The Minus Side[/b] [b]The Learning Wall:[/b] The game is very "hostile" to new players at the start. You will die—a lot—before the mechanics truly click. [b]Environmental Variety:[/b] After several hours, the tilesets and backgrounds start to feel repetitive. A few more distinct biomes would help keep the journey fresh. [b]Bare-Bones UI:[/b] The user interface is functional, but it feels a bit clinical and "early access." It could use some more visual flair to match the cool art style of the characters. [b]Final Verdict[/b] Turnbound is a "tough but fair" gem. It’s perfect for the "one more turn" type of gamer who enjoys the challenge of a digital tabletop experience. It has a very specific soul that is hard to find in bigger, more bloated RPGs. [i]I’ve been closely watching the development of Turnbound, and the polish on the combat loop is impressive. I’d love to receive a key for the upcoming full release or DLC to see how the world and enemy variety expand from here![/i]

Absolute recommend. It says 14 hours on record, but it doesnt count the 50 I have from the demo. I tried the demo from a crossover with a different game, thinking hah ten minutes and then I will get a random cosmetic reward and move on with my life. Well, here I am, having followed early access closely and excited for the launch of 1.0! Its a gripping game that is absolutely worth giving a try if the genre speaks to you. The devs listen to the community and care a lot, there has been so much balancing and adjusting since the demo. The game has a ranked and non-ranked system if the rng gets too bad for you. There is a bit of a skill issue there but hey not everyone is a top tier strategist who plays the system like a pro, and even for those people (myself included) there are options to have hours of non-competitive fun, try out strats in peace and slowly improve if that is something you want. Plus I saw people complaining about the rng of which tile roles first, the game has a reroll button for this system if you feel a particular round was unfair. The characters each offer a really unique way to play while retaining some general overlap. The designs are great and the little cosmetic additions you can unlock that have been added since the demo make it all the more enjoyable to play this game. It just is a really fun game, go give it a try!

There are some games which trigger me hard, and this is one of them. IMHO it's really new player unfriendly. Why are there no hover-over descriptions of effects/buffs? Things like "confuses a weapon". Like thanks for nothing. WTF is a confused weapon? Also a good one: "Coin mark". That name is cleary self explanatory. Or "Aura:". What's an aura? Apparently is seems to be an effect that is repeatedly applied each turn. And the RNGness is annoying. You start with Alice and you rolled no weapon in the first round? First round already lost. And then there is no clear order in which things are targeted. If you're lucky and hit the enemys main damage weapon you might win the fight with hardly any loss. You replay the same fight, and you loose hard because before mentioned weapon was not targeted.

★★★★★ — Addictive and Impossible to Walk Away From I got pulled into Turnbound by watching my favorite streamers play it before release, and the moment I got my hands on it I was completely hooked. The tile-based inventory battler concept sounds deceptively simple, but the depth of combos and synergies you can build across each run is endlessly fascinating. The ability to save runs and share them with friends and communities is a fantastic way to show off your best builds. I picked up some incredible tricks just by studying how the community optimized their boards for each of the three heroes. Play as Alice, Sun Wukong, or Robin Hood, each bringing their own unique flair to your strategy as you battle through randomized opponents.

Turnbound is one of those games that's easy to pick up but difficult to put down. I often find myself returning to play a another match...and another...and then another ^.^ The real fun comes in buying tiles, organizing your board, discovering synergies between tiles and then creating a truly monstrous board! Smart, tactical tile placement will be the key to victory.

Game is terribly balanced. You can stack attack sky high so item HP is irrelevant and basically everything gets one shotted making big chunk of items worthless since they require items to get damaged and not destroyed. Character abilities range from useless to OP too. Like Alice white rabbit just lets you snowball super hard while Kitsune requires destroying items with burn which is almost nigh impossible leaving the ability useless.

Game is fun, looks great, and the noise the tiles make when you hover over them is ridiculously satisfying. I spent 30 seconds just doing circles with my cursor on the board lol. These types of games are all about synergies and thoughtful tile placement, and it's clear that the depth is there even after only playing 3 runs. Saw another review complain that the game is "beginner unfriendly" and it really got me scratching my head. That's really not the case. The tutorial tells you everything you need to know, the tooltips are great, and there's a question mark icon in the top right corner that explains every keyword. I really don't see the issue. My only gripe so far is that you can lose a battle, hit replay and then win it. It doesn't feel right to me that the person with the better build doesn't always win, and I say that knowing that I would probably end up losing more if that were the case anyways lol. Maybe this is actually a player friendly design choice despite it not seeming that way at first glance? I don't know how big of an issue it is within the current playerbase, if some other elegant solution exists or even if the devs consider this rng aspect an important part of what makes it fun, but as of right now, with only about 4 hours of playtime, I see it as a small detriment to the overall experience. I guess I'll edit this if my thoughts change after playing it some more. I really don't want to leave the review on a negative note though, game is great, would recommend!

探索机制还是能消遣部分时间，合成升级的机制还算有意思，所以给个好评，但是玩下来还是觉得有很多别扭的地方 策略性总体来说，容错太低，且很依赖运气。物品和加强是纯随机，物价又很高，回合金又很少，又要用来解锁格子，而因为物价高和纯随机，导致刷新商店变成了性价比极低的操作。导致经常运气不好接连几个回合都是零提升。另外部分流派极度依赖某一个核心物品，刷不到一局铺垫都白做。合成虽然能够掉落随机物品，但是需要花费合成金且掉落物品随机，导致初期到后期的过渡变得很别扭，低等级非核心的过渡物品不合成赢不了对局，到不了后期，合成了卖价又很低，经济崩盘后期根本没法转型高等级物品。 总结的话，整体感受太多的随机感觉玩起来像个赌徒游戏，刷不出核心只能恶心到死，且因为回合金和物价高、刷新纯随机等等因素，每回合能干的事很少，整体没什么参与感，只有商店刷出东西才能爽一下，纯看商店脸色了。

This game is pretty good and I enjoy playing it a reasonable amount. However there are a few issues that are large enough for me not to recommend the game considering its at full launch. If steam had a "mixed" option for recommendations I would have picked that. I have experience with multiple auto battlers, having been high rated in TFT and the Bazaar, which this game seems to be heavily influenced by. The game balance is not great, there are a few builds that are just much better to go with, leaving less room for experimentation if you are actually playing to win. Also the fact that oftentimes the game can be determined by a coin flip for who moves first, instead of what other auto-battlers have done with an attack speed or priority system on the individual tiles themselves is a negative as well. The biggest issue that I have the game and the reason I decided to not recommend the game, is the fact that core builds are locked behind a leveling mechanism. In a PVE game this would be fine but considering the game is entirely PVP, although asynchronous, it just means you are gating a large amount of the content and builds behind arbitrary levels that don't really do too much other than give you less content, initially.

I'm pretty sad to give this game a thumbs down but they've really made some huge mistakes in the design that really ruin the gameplay via EXCESSIVE rng. 1. Instead of real time combat like other auto battlers they went with turn based. Unfortunately with this kind of game that gives a huge advantage to whoever goes first. 2. If that wasn't enough RNG they don't have a universal health pool. Instead pieces are attacked randomly and destroyed. 3. The third and final nail is that you lose when your hero dies. There are ways to protect it but you really can just get "lucky" and beat the opponent instantly if you break that defense and target the hero through RNG. They have systems to mitigate all of this of course. You can get echos to redo the combat to get a different result. I think for people who seriously enjoy auto battlers though this is just too much RNG. I hope they look at changing the basic mechanics to possibly lower the RNG factors.

The game needs lots of work still, cannot recommend in its current state. While the game shows potential and is initially interesting, the flow of the game is just "off". It is far too RNG dependent at several critical junctions, such as coin flip for first, shop items, opponent matching, all attacks being random, etc, the game just feels hollow, win or lose. There is a "rematch" option( only 2 available per run) and you almost always get a different result when it is close, further emphasizing how much its just a coin flip whether you won or lost in the first place. I have gone 10-0 several times, so no I'm not talking about "skill issue". There is a lack of variety in cards, synergies, game balance, etc. etc. I could go on, game just still needs a lot of work, and I am worried that because it looks good, and already early release, that the devs may not continue the game to completion, because it isn't there yet.

It´s a hard one. The game itself is like Backpackbattles and the Artstyle is quite nice. It´s engaging and can bring a lot of fun. The pacing is nice and there are enough Combos to entertain you for a while. But after you understand the system it´s quite hard to stay calm. While i, for example, like to play Robin Hood and know there are some item´s that grant you attack and health, 99% of the time you don´t get them early. So when you start a battle after Day 3, the enemies weapons often have like 11 Attack and 28 Health (11/28) While you have a Bow with 4 attack and 6 life (4/6), which, when you do it clever, can go up to like (8/12), which is still no match for the enemy weapons which have those Items BASELINE. The random attack also doesn´t help. Sometimes your Taunt items actually taunt and make the enemy attack it until it´s dead consecutively, but sometimes, without any effect procced, they suddenly ignore this item and attack your Hero for example, which is very strange. There doesn´t seem to be a system behind it. Thorns are also extremely op. Often you have glasscannon weapons which you can´t change so quickly and you loose your entire Arsenal of weapons while not even having a single item of the enemy down, which is nowhere close to being balanced. The game has a LOT of potential, but needs a lot of polishing done.

[h1]Context[/h1] [list] [*]Played this game demo a lot, when there were only 2 classes and was excited about the potential of a full release. [*]After the release there were only 2 classes added, a few balance changes and not really a lot of new items. [*]So after playing for a few hours after release I'm inclined to pause it for now and perhaps return some time later. [/list] [h1]Overview[/h1] [list] [*]Style felt very good, flavor-win has it's place here. [*]Visual elements and board/space mechanic of the game felt great. [*]Shop and level up mechanics feel good and thought out. [*]Auto-battling mechanics - felt a little too random for my taste (especially with the token to re-run the match potentially with the new result, it just screams you in the face - you were unlucky, bite it). [/list] [h1]Summary[/h1] The game was and is still a solidly built auto-battler with cool mechanics and a really good style. For me it was a good experience and I would recommend it, with a "but" for now: there is just too little stuff to do as of now, many subclasses that got introduced on the release are under-pushed and kinda don't matter, there are too few items for each strategy presented to us (or they're weak). After a couple of updates I would definitely give it another try and see what the devs got cooking, this has great potential. I wish them good luck!
